overview.text: A glacier is a long-lasting mass of land ice—often mixed with snow, rock, and sediment—that forms where snowfall builds up faster than it melts. Gravity makes the ice flow downhill: ice crystals deform internally, and the glacier may also slide over or shear its bed. Debris trapped in the ice grinds and plucks rock, carving features such as U-shaped valleys and cirques. As ice melts, it leaves debris, including ridges called moraines, while meltwater can carry and sort sediment farther away. A glacier’s end can advance or retreat as its gains and losses change, but the ice continues to flow. Glaciers reshape terrain and store freshwater.

key_facts.text: Glaciers form where snow accumulation exceeds melting; accumulated snow is compressed into ice.
Glacier movement combines deformation within the ice with motion at its base, such as sliding or shearing sediment.
Abrasion grinds and scratches bedrock; plucking removes rock chunks that the ice can carry.
Moraines are piles of sediment deposited by glaciers; meltwater can transport and rework sediment as outwash.
A glacier’s terminus may retreat while its ice keeps flowing downhill; retreat happens when melting exceeds accumulation.
